title: App Switcher Returns in watchOS 27.2 Beta With New Launch Gesture
content:
Apple has apparently listened to user feedback and brought back the App Switcher screen in the latest watchOS 27.2 beta, but accessing it is a little different than before.


In watchOS 26 and earlier versions, a double press of the Digital Crown would bring up the App Switcher, where you could easily switch to the last-used app and view and open other recently used apps. You could also swipe left on a misbehaving app to force close it. 

Live Rewind AI feature, so it no longer brings up the App Switcher screen. There were concerns that this meant the App Switcher would be gone for good, but Apple has reinstated it in the second watchOS 27.2 beta, released yesterday. 

The gesture for opening it has changed, though.

As shown in the video below, you now access the App Switcher by pressing and holding the bottom of the screen while you're in an app.

Apple has brought back the App Switcher!
On watchOS 26 and earlier, you could access the App Switcher by double-clicking the Digital Crown, then turning the Digital Crown to navigate through your recently used apps. You could also swipe left on an app and tap the "X" button to... pic.twitter.com/G5fa0TeTR9
—  (@limpless_skelly) September 22, 2026
 

Apple says Live Rewind, which which offers a transcript of what was said in the last 15 seconds, will be available later this year on Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

title: Apple Music Hall Spatial Audio Venue Opens in Battersea Power Station
content:
Apple has announced the opening of Apple Music Hall, a state-of-the-art 600-capacity music venue located in London's Battersea Power Station. Apple says it is "designed to connect artists and fans through bespoke, intimate performances unlike anywhere else."


Apple says the hall incorporates heritage brickwork, fluted arches, and bronze balconies reminiscent of the historic oriel windows, while a giant glass wall "further enhances the visual connection with the historic building, offering a panoramic view of the concourse and the river beyond."

The 38-foot-wide stage can be reconfigured for traditional front-facing sets or more in-the-round experiences, and a 48-speaker spatial sound system is positioned all around the audience. Behind the stage is a dedicated recording and mix studio so that every performance can be captured as a multi-track recording and mixed in Spatial Audio, live or in post-production.


The venue is also hardwired for 16 or more cameras that feed a purpose-built broadcast control room with infrastructure that supports iPhone video capture running in parallel alongside traditional broadcast cameras.

The exhaustive setup means artists can perform a live show, record it in Spatial Audio, create a broadcast-ready mix, and capture multicamera video – all directly in the venue.


Apple says performances out of Apple Music Hall will also be livestreamed globally so fans outside of London can tune in to enjoy shows from their favorite artists. For more information about Apple Music Hall, including tickets for upcoming shows, fans can visit applemusichall.com or follow @applemusichall on Instagram and TikTok.

title: Apple CEO John Ternus Talks iPhone Duo Design, Siri AI, and Becoming CEO
content:
Apple CEO John Ternus did an interview with Canal+ talk show Clique following Apple's September event. He discussed the iPhone Duo's design, difficulties Apple ran into when developing it, his plans for Apple, and more.



On the design of the ‌iPhone Duo‌, Ternus explained why Apple went with an iPad-like shape when the device is unfolded.
I think it's something new and unique, right? But I think we didn't want to just do what we'd seen other people do, which is sort of take two phone shapes and stick them together and then you get this weird square thing. We came at it from we want to build a large screen experience that feels right to us. And obviously we've been doing that for a long time with iPad. And so we knew kind of the shape, you know, we came up with this new aspect ratio.

Ternus said that when developing the ‌iPhone Duo‌, there were "so many problems" to solve, but a foldable was an opportunity for Apple employees to "be really clever" and "come up with entirely new things." He said some of the hardware engineering problems Apple had to address involved the design of the hinge and the display, and making them reliable.

When asked to share his favorite ‌iPhone Duo‌ trick, Ternus showed off the device's opening animation. "I mean, this is really fun, you know, the animation that you get as you open it across from one side to the other. It's just sort of whimsical and fun. And it brings a smile to your face."

Siri AI is "not designed to be your friend," which is something we heard earlier this year from Craig Federighi. Ternus said Apple doesn't want to replace human relationships. "They're how we learn, they're how we grow, they're how we find joy and happiness," he said.

Tim Cook and Apple's board asked Ternus if he wanted to be the next Apple CEO. Ternus didn't say when he was approached, but he said the question came as a surprise. "When Tim asked me if it was something I would consider, I would say the good news is I was sitting down, because I never in a million years would have imagined that happening," said Ternus.

As Apple's CEO, Ternus said he doesn't have plans for a radical change. He was asked if Apple was going back to its roots under his leadership, with more of a focus on engineering products.
I don't think anything's really changed. Sure, I'm new in this job, but the focus on innovation, the focus on products, the focus most importantly on our customers, that has never changed. That's been here from the beginning.


Ternus said it was "amazing" to be able to say "one more thing" on stage at Apple's September event. "I've seen Steve say it, and I've seen Tim say it," he said. "And so having the opportunity for me to say it was pretty magical. Kind of goosebumps."

full interview includes Ternus' thoughts on ‌Tim Cook‌, the AI race, Apple's environmental goals, the Vision Pro, the new parental controls added in iOS 27, and more.

title: You Can No Longer Downgrade From iOS 27 to iOS 26
content:
Apple is no longer signing iOS 26.6.2, so if you've upgraded to iOS 27, there is no option to downgrade to a version of iOS 26. ‌iOS 27‌ came out a week ago.


Software that is "signed" can pass a server-side verification check that Apple performs when a new version of iOS is downloaded. If an update fails the verification check, it can't be installed.

By unsigning software, Apple prevents customers from installing outdated, less secure versions of iOS.

title: macOS 27.2 Beta Brings New Volume and Brightness Sliders
content:
With the second beta of macOS Golden Gate 27.2, Apple updated the look of the volume and brightness sliders when you adjust them with the keyboard.


The new sliders have a segmented bar instead of a plain line, making it clearer how much each key press adjusts volume or brightness. Apple used a similar design in macOS Sequoia before Liquid Glass, and the new look is a cross between the old slider and the Liquid Glass slider.

There are no longer two icons at the beginning and end of the slider, and Apple now uses a single larger icon on the left. The sliders appear where a matching menu bar icon is located, so if you have a dedicated sound icon, the slider shows up below it.

title: Latest macOS beta: What’s new and should you install it?
content:
Macworld





Apple released macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14, 2026, but development hasn’t stopped. Just two days later on September 16, Apple issued the first developer beta of macOS 27.2, beginning testing of the operating system’s next major point update. Yes, that’s macOS 27.2, not macOS 27.1. 
The macOS 27.2 beta gives developers and testers early access to Apple’s latest fixes, refinements and any features that weren’t ready for the initial Golden Gate release. 
However, as with any beta software, it may introduce bugs, compatibility problems and poorer battery life so we recommend caution if you wish to install it.
Here’s everything you need to know about the latest macOS beta, including what’s new, when the next public beta is likely to arrive and whether you should install it.


What’s the latest macOS beta? 
Apple offers two beta streams: a developer beta and a public beta. The public beta allows enthusiasts and early adopters to test upcoming changes before they are released to everyone. You need to join Apple’s Beta Software Program to access it.
The latest Mac beta is macOS 27.2 beta 2, which Apple released to registered developers on September 21, 2026. It arrived less than a weekbeta 1.
The corresponding macOS 27.2 public beta is expected shortly. Public betas usually follow developer betas, although Apple does not guarantee a particular schedule.
macOS 27 Golden Gate beta version tracker 
Apple released macOS 27.2 Golden Gate Developer Beta 2 on September 21, 2026.
The macOS 27.2 Golden Gate Public Beta 2 should be released sometime the same week; new versions are usually released a day or two after the new developer beta.
macOS 26 Tahoe beta: Apple may continue updating macOS 26 Tahoe with security and maintenance releases, but macOS 27 is now the current operating system and the focus of Apple’s beta program.

What’s new in the latest beta?

				
					

				
			
New features in macOS 27.

Foundry




Apple has not announced any major consumer-facing additions in macOS 27.2 beta 2. The following changes are expected though:
Bug fixes and performance improvements: Addressing issues in the first release of macOS 27.
Additional Siri AI languages: Apple has said the Siri AI will expand to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish in October. 
Automatic password changes: The promised feature that automatically changes compromised passwords has not yet been implemented, but it could arrive in macOS 27.2.. 
We’ll update this section as changes are discovered.
See Apple’s developer website for more information about the beta. 


						

							


Should you install the macOS beta?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Installing the macOS beta lets you test Apple’s next round of features, fixes and refinements before their public release. Most Mac users should remain on the standard version of macOS 27, particularly if they rely on their Mac for work.
Install if…
You need to test apps
You want early access to new features
You have a secondary Mac available
Wait if…
This is your primary work machine
You rely on niche or specialist software
Stability is critical to your workflow


						

							






Who are you Should you install?

A developer testing appsConsider the developer beta
An enthusiast with a spare MacConsider the public beta 
General user with one MacStay on macOS 27

 






What are the risks of installing beta software?
Installing pre-release software on a primary device carries several risks.
System instability: Performance problems, freezes, crashes, and other unexpected behavior are common during beta testing.
App failures: Third-party applications may crash, behave unpredictably, or stop working entirely.
Hardware strain: Early beta builds can increase battery drain and cause Macs to run hotter than usual.
Data loss: Software bugs may corrupt files, and downgrading to a stable version often requires a complete system reset.


						

							


Safety precautions and best practices
If you decide to install the beta, take the following precautions:
Use a secondary device: Avoid installing beta software on your primary Mac or on any machine used for critical work.
Create a full backup: Use Time Machine to create a complete backup before upgrading so you can restore your Mac if something goes wrong. Note that this needs to be a Time Machine backup from before the beta was installed and you will lose anything saved subsequently.
Install on a separate volume: Consider installing the beta on a separate volume or external SSD rather than replacing your main operating system.
Check storage space: Make sure you have at least 15GB of free storage available before beginning the installation.


						

							


How to install the macOS beta

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The process for installing a macOS beta depends on whether you are seeking the Developer Beta or the Public Beta. Apple simplified this process a few years ago, removing the need for a paid developer account to access early builds. 
The first step is to join Apple’s beta testing program. We explain how to do that in a separate article.
You will need to register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac.
To install the beta follow these steps:
Back up your Mac: Before installing any pre-release software, it is critical to prepare your Mac to avoid data loss. Beta software is inherently unstable and can cause crashes or app compatibility issues. 
Register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac:
For the Public Beta: Visit the Apple Beta Software Program website, sign in with your Apple ID, and agree to the terms.
For the Developer Beta: Register as an Apple Developer on Apple’s website, download the Apple Developer app from the App Store, sign in with your standard Apple ID, and complete the free registration process.
On the Mac where you wish to install the beta, open System Settings and navigate to General > Software Update.
Click the (i) info button next to Beta Updates.
Enable Beta Updates.
The beta will appear as an available upgrade. Select the macOS beta you want to install (e.g., macOS Public Beta or Developer Beta).
Click Upgrade Now to begin the download and installation.
As long as you are a registered developer or enrolled in the public beta program, when the relevant macOS Beta becomes available, it will also show up on your Mac.
Once you are running the beta, the updates will come through to your Mac automatically; you just need to go to Software Update in System Settings and click to install. See How to install macOS.


						

							


How to get a free Apple developer account
If you just want a free Apple Developer account so you can access the beta, you can get this via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app on an iPhone:
Get the Apple Developer App from the App Store. 
Open the app on your iPhone. 
Tap on Account. 
Tap on Sign In. 
Sign in using your usual Apple ID. 
If you wish to actually publish applications to the App Store or receive support, you’ll need to pay $99/£79 per year for a paid account. You can compare the free and paid accounts here.


						

							





 FAQ 


1.
Who can run the macOS beta?
Anyone can run the macOS beta, but to do so, you do need to register for either the developer beta, the public beta, or both.
Apple offers both developer and public beta programs for macOS, enabling all interested users to test pre-release versions of the operating system. While both betas provide early access to new features, they cater to different user profiles based on technical expertise and risk tolerance. Beta software tends to be buggy so the more stable public beta version may be preferable, but even that will not be bug-free.
In the past, the developer beta was only available to developers who had paid to join Apple’s Developer Program (which costs $99/£79). However, for a couple of years now, Apple has opened up the developer beta to registered developers with free developer accounts. We explain how to get a free developer account below. 
If you decide you no longer want to run the beta version of macOS read this: How to remove the macOS beta.





2.
macOS public beta vs developer beta
Since 2023, the Developer Beta has been available to anyone who registers as a developer, even if they aren’t a paid-up member of Apple’s Developer Program. As a result, people with a basic free developer account can download the new macOS developer beta (we show you how to register below).
Whether you should download the developer beta if you aren’t a developer is another question. We don’t recommend you install the developer beta if you aren’t a developer. Instead, our recommendation is to use the public beta (the first version of which usually arrives in July).
There are a few differences between the public and developer betas. The public beta is not the same as the beta that is released through the developer program. The public beta typically launches after the developer beta has undergone initial testing and refinement
Developers get updates to their beta first, and possibly more frequently. But you should keep in mind that betas are by nature not stable, and because the public beta comes after the developer beta it could be a little safer to install. 
The most significant difference is probably the motive of the testers: Developers usually have the aim of ensuring their apps work when the updated macOS is released to the general public, while public beta testers are essentially helping Apple detect bugs and offering feedback on the features. Because of this, developers may get to test new features not available in the public beta. 
If you want to get the public beta the first thing you need to do, if you haven’t already, is join Apple’s beta programs read this for more information: How to become an Apple beta tester.





3.
Is the macOS beta stable?
By its nature, a beta has the potential to be unstable. Therefore, it’s not advised that you install it on a Mac that you rely on. If you have a second Mac that isn’t mission-critical, then install it there. We strongly recommend that you don’t risk all by putting the macOS beta on your primary Mac, especially not in the early days of the beta development. 
If you don’t have a second Mac, there are a couple of ways you could run macOS beta on your Mac without running the risk of losing data or finding your Mac stops working:
We recommend installing it on a partition, which these days is really a volume (and is much easier to create than a partition was). Read about how to do that here: How to dual-boot Mac: Run two versions of macOS on a Mac.
Alternatively, you could install the macOS beta on an external drive and run it on that.
We discuss the safety of the macOS beta and the risks you might be taking in more detail in a separate article.





4.
How to prepare your Mac for the beta
Update your software: We recommend you have the latest full version of macOS installed, although Apple says that the macOS Developer Beta Access Utility requires macOS 10.8 or later.
Make space: We’d recommend at least 25-30GB of available space because the macOS betas tend to be very large. If you end up requiring more space, read: How to free up space on Mac. Note that we always recommend that you have at least 10% space free on your Mac at any time, so if you don’t have that, expect problems!
Back up: Before you install a beta on your Mac, you should make a backup of your data and files. You can find out how to use Time Machine to back up your Mac. We also have a round-up of suitable backup solutions.





5.
How to send feedback to Apple
Should you come across an error or a bug, you should use the Feedback Assistant app to provide feedback to Apple. Launch the app and follow the appropriate steps, selecting the area about which you’re providing feedback and then any specific sub-area. Then describe your issue in a single sentence, before providing a more detailed description, including any specific steps that reproduce the issue. You’ll also be able to attach other files.
You’ll also have to give permission for the Feedback Assistant app to collect diagnostic information from your Mac.
It won’t always be obvious whether something is a bug or just not as easy to use as you might have hoped. Either way, if your feedback is that something appears to work in an illogical way, Apple will want to know that.
If you are having trouble with a third-party app, you can let Apple know by reporting it through the 3rd-party Application Compatibility category in the Feedback Assistant. However, we’d suggest that you also provide feedback to the app’s developer, who will no doubt be grateful.





6.
Will I be able to update from macOS beta to the final version?
Beta users can move to the finished release once its build is newer than – or equivalent to – the beta installed. Read: How to leave the macOS beta.  





7.
Can I talk about the beta publicly?
According to Apple and the license agreement all beta testers must agree to, the beta is “Apple confidential information”. By accepting those terms, you agree not to discuss your use of the software with anyone who isn’t also in the Beta Software Program. That means you can’t “blog, post screenshots, tweet, or publicly post information about the public beta software.”
However, you can discuss any information that Apple has publicly disclosed; the company says that information is no longer considered confidential.





8.
How to downgrade from the macOS beta
You can always revert to an earlier version of macOS, though depending on how you back up, it’s not necessarily a painless process.
Start by making sure the data on your drive is backed up, then erase the drive and install the latest public version of macOS. When you first start up your Mac, you can use the Migration Assistant to import your data from the backup. Here’s a more detailed tutorial on downgrading from the macOS beta and we also have a tutorial on downgrading to an older version of the Mac OS.





9.
Is the beta free to download? 
Yes, the macOS beta is free to download for both developers and the general public. Apple offers two distinct tracks for testing pre-release software: the Developer Beta and the Public Beta, both of which are now accessible without a paid subscription.





10.
Can I go back to the stable version?
Yes, you can go back to the stable version of macOS from a beta, but the complexity of the process depends on whether the final version of that software has been released yet.
If you are running macOS 27.2 beta and want to return to the current public release of macOS 27, simply turning off Beta Updates will stop future beta installations, but it will not immediately downgrade the Mac. To return before Apple releases an equivalent public build, you may need to erase the Mac and reinstall macOS, then restore data from a backup made before installing the beta.





11.
Should I install the beta on my main Mac?
Installing a macOS beta on your primary computer is generally not recommended due to the inherent risks of using unfinished software. While beta programs offer early access to new features, they are designed for testing and often contain significant bugs that can disrupt your daily workflow.





12.
Do I need an Apple Developer account to install the beta?
You do not need a paid Apple Developer account to install the macOS beta. While access to developer betas was previously restricted to those paying a $99/£79 annual fee, Apple changed this policy in 2023 to allow anyone with a free developer account to access these builds. Alternatively, you can join the Public Beta program, which is also free and accessible to anyone with a valid Apple ID.





13.
How often are new beta versions released?
New macOS beta versions are typically released every one to two weeks, with the frequency increasing as the final public release date approaches. The beta updates refine features and address bugs identified by testers.





14.
Is the macOS beta safe to install?
The beta is generally safe to test, but it may contain bugs that cause crashes, poor battery life, app compatibility issues, or data loss. Always back up your Mac before installing.





15.
Will my apps work with the macOS beta?
Many apps will work normally, but some third-party software may crash, perform poorly, or not launch at all until developers release updates.

title: GM Wants You to Know It Still Plans to Ditch Apple CarPlay in Future EVs
content:
Recent reports claiming that General Motors is reversing course on its controversial plans to ditch CarPlay in its future EVs appear to be incorrect.


As noted by Joanna Stern, host of the YouTube channel New Things, a GM spokesperson has confirmed that its new software interface that shows CarPlay or Android Auto alongside its own native system in 2027 models of its Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra is specific to the gas-powered versions of those pickup trucks.

GM previously stated that CarPlay and Android Auto would continue to be offered in its new gas-powered vehicles for the "foreseeable future," so the 2027 models of those trucks still supporting those platforms is not a change of course.

There is one more wrinkle in that GM's all-electric 2027 Cadillac LYRIQ supports CarPlay and Android Auto still — it is unclear if the Lyriq will always be an exception or if it will simply be one of GM's final EVs to ever support phone mirroring systems. Overall, though, GM continues to insist that its future EVs will not offer CarPlay.

title: iOS 27.2 beta 2 is out now, skipping over iOS 27.1
content:
Macworld





Just a couple days after the wide release of iOS 27, Apple has released the first beta of iOS 27.2. That’s not a typo: it’s iOS 27.2, not 27.1. We never saw a 27.1 release, but Apple is beginning beta tests for the 27.2 branch.
This likely has something to do with the iPhone Duo, which is going on sale in October. We know the iPhone Duo will come with iOS 27.1, but we don’t yet know if any other devices will ever get a 27.1 update, or when all the devices will get on the same version together.
Update September 21: The second beta release is out now, less than a week after the first. 
What’s new in iOS 27.2
As beta testers report new capabilities in this version, we’ll report them here. 
New Health app: The 27.2 beta includes the new Health app, with a totally new redesign and AI-powered health insights.
Siri AI languages: Apple said that Siri AI, which launched supporting only U.S. English, will expand to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
Dual Capture for Group FaceTime: Users can stream their front and rear cameras at the same time during FaceTime calls.
Podcasts Up Next: Up Next has been refreshed with two rows at the top of the Home tab: New Episodes and Continue Playing.
Simple Profiles on iOS/iPadOS/web: The Apple TV feature that lets you use multiple different account profiles now works in the Apple TV app on iOS, iPadOS, and the web.
Multiview in Apple TV: The feature that lets you watch four select sports streams at the same time on Apple TV now works on the Apple TV app on iOS.
iOS 27.2: How to install the public beta
If you want to test the iOS 27 beta releases but are not a registered developer, follow these steps:
Click Sign Up on the Apple Beta page and register with your Apple ID.
Log in to the Beta Software Program.
Click Enroll your iOS device.
Open the Settings app, tap General, then Software Update.
In the Beta Updates section, select the iOS Public Beta.
It may take a few moments after registering for the beta option to appear in Software Update.
iOS 27.2: How to install the developer beta
You’ll need to be registered as an Apple developer, but a free developer account will do. You can get one via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app:
Download the Apple Developer App from the App Store.
Open the app.
Tap on Account.
Sign in using your usual Apple ID.

Sold directly by Apple


Current purchase prices depend on third-party stock, condition, and warranty
iPhone 18 Pro: From $49.95 a month for 24 months via Apple Upgrade
iPhone 18 Pro Max: From $54.12 a month for 24 months via Apple Upgrade




For iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 14 Pro Max owners considering a new device, the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ is a worthwhile upgrade. Four generations of changes bring improvements to the display, every camera on the device, battery life, charging, sustained performance, and connectivity. Battery life is likely to be the strongest improvement for most users, particularly if their current device no longer comfortably lasts through the day, while faster wired charging makes brief charging stops more useful. The newer battery is also designed to retain 80% of its original capacity for twice as many complete charge cycles under ideal conditions, and Charge Limit offers more control over long-term battery wear.

USB-C is another significant quality-of-life improvement for iPhone 14 Pro owners. It allows the iPhone to share cables with recent Macs, iPads, and accessories, while the jump from USB 2 to USB 3 speeds makes large wired photo and video transfers far quicker. The Action button and Camera Control also provide two new physical controls that the iPhone 14 Pro lacks.

The camera upgrade is especially compelling for anyone who regularly takes photos or records video. Higher-resolution Ultra Wide and Telephoto cameras expand the options beyond the Main camera, while the variable aperture and Pro controls provide additional creative flexibility. Both iPhone 14 Pro sizes move from a 3x Telephoto camera to 4x, alongside an optical-quality 8x option that substantially extends their usable reach.

Apple Vision Pro owners. The square front-camera sensor makes landscape framing easier without rotating the phone, while Center Stage improves flexibility for group photos and video calls.

The A20 Pro and vapor chamber cooling make the strongest performance case for users who play demanding games, record long video clips, or regularly push their device through sustained workloads. The increase from 6GB to 12GB of RAM and the additional AI processing hardware also enable ‌Apple Intelligence‌, ‌Siri‌ AI, and ‌Visual Intelligence‌, none of which are available on the iPhone 14 Pro. The older model still supports ‌iOS 27‌ and remains capable for messaging, browsing, photography, and other everyday activities, so the latest software update does not make it obsolete.

There are physical trade-offs to consider. Both newer models are taller and thicker, although the move from stainless steel to aluminum means the weight increases by only 5 grams on the Pro and 9 grams on the Pro Max despite the larger displays and batteries. The aluminum enclosure improves thermal management, but it is less premium-looking, and it may show dents and scratches more readily than the iPhone 14 Pro's stainless steel frame.

If your iPhone 14 Pro still meets your needs and comfortably lasts through the day, upgrading is not urgent, but you may want to think about getting a new device soon. A battery replacement may be worth considering if reduced health is your main complaint and you would otherwise be happy to keep your device. The upgrade becomes much easier to recommend when battery limitations coincide with a desire for ‌Apple Intelligence‌, USB-C, the newer cameras, and a larger display.

title: iPhone 18 Pro owners report two serious bugs causing freezes and restarts
content:
Macworld





Apple upped the price of its phones this year, and while the new iPhone 18 Pro doesn’t cost quite as much as its Max sibling (let alone the $1,999+ iPhone Duo) it’s in the premium bracket where everything needs to be perfect. And sadly, that doesn’t appear to be the case.
The 18 Pro went on sale on Friday (triggering a heartening amount of customer hype) and two bugs have already been reported.
Frozen screen bug
Alleged bug number one: in some cases and at some times, the iPhone 18 Pro’s screen is believed to stop responding to touch. One owner posted a video of this behavior to Twitter/X; their thumb appears to swipe up and down on the display (while using a social media app, possibly Twitter), yet nothing happens in response.


iPhone 18 Pro randomly stops responding to touch 😭 pic.twitter.com/xr76g6OyHc
— Noah Cat (@Cartidise) September 20, 2026





When a commenter on the post claimed that this is a bug in iOS 27 rather than the iPhone 18 Pro, and that the poster “swiped down both Notification Center and Control Center at the same time which causes the phone to freeze,” the poster responded that they didn’t “exploit any bug” and that the problem has happened twice already. Then they link to a second user reporting the same issue.
We’ve also seen a similar complaint about touch sensitivity on Reddit, although this might have a different cause; the owner mentions use of a screen protector.
Face ID bug
Alleged bug number two: a Face ID bug has caused some iPhone 18 Pro handsets to freeze and then reboot. What appears to happen is that when a Face ID verification fails, the behavior triggers.
A thread on Reddit contains the following complaint: “Not even 24 hours and I have my 18 Pro Max panic restarting. Three times due to Face ID and one by some timeout (whilst loading Apple Wallet). Called Apple support, done a Face ID reset after three restarts.”
Of the 24 direct responses from other users, 22 confirm that they’ve experienced the same or a similar issue. Some speculate (as we saw with the touch sensitivity bug) that it could be an issue with iOS 27 or other software rather than the new hardware. As evidenced by the testimony of one commenter and the original poster, the bug affects the 18 Pro Max as well as the 18 Pro.
As 9to5Mac notes in its coverage of this second bug, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max feature a redesigned, smaller Face ID sensor array, which may be at the root of the issue. The site speculates that there may be a glitch in the section of iOS 27 which relates to this specific piece of hardware.
The original poster of the Reddit thread, however, reports that after they got in touch with Apple support, the company ran diagnostics and decided that it was a faulty unit.
Macworld can’t confirm the existence of these bugs. But these aren’t one-off complaints; multiple customers report each of the problems, which makes it unlikely that they’re imaginary. In the case of the Face ID bug, Macworld readers may be able to reproduce the behavior for themselves by attempting to unlock a protected app or document (such as a locked note in Notes) and then obscuring their face so it fails.
If these do turn out to be legitimate bugs they will join a long list of post-launch iPhone complaints, including Antennagate in 2010 and Bendgate in 2014. Last year we had Scratchgate, which didn’t go viral in the same way but caused a fuss for a while, and an issue with photos having small blacked-out portions. That second one was officially acknowledged by Apple; it remains to be seen how the company will respond to these latest reports.
creator: Macworld

title: The Glacier iPhone 18 Pro Max is the anti-Cosmic Orange
content:
Macworld





I have an iPhone 18 Pro Max. Its color finish is Glacier. And I am of a generation that uses the term “cool” as a way to show approval, even if over the years, “cool” has gone from an enthusiastic expression to a subdued feeling.
When it comes to my reaction to the Glacier iPhone 18 Pro Max, the first word I turn to is “cool.” I want to think it deserves a better word, but I can’t think of one. Glacier is cool because my reaction to it is cool, too. It’s nice, pretty, even. And though calling Glacier “cool” seems a bit on-the-nose, it fits.

				
					

				
			The cool and the hot of iPhone color theory.
Foundry




But as I said, “cool” is subdued, and that’s how I feel about it. It’s not slap-you-in-the-face, look-at-me-I-said-look-at-me like Cosmic Orange. Cosmic Orange is not cool. Cosmic Orange is hot, in a Paris Hilton way.
Oh, Cosmic Orange. How I adore Cosmic Orange. In a world where black, gray, and white dominate smartphones, Cosmic Orange stands out with pride. A flex, even–when you see it, those who know, know. 

				
					

				
			
Foundry




There’s another reason why I enjoy Cosmic Orange. It’s a callback to the fun times of the original iMac, the Bondi Blue statement that shook up technology. How dare Apple give a computer some personality! We loved it. Cosmic Orange brought that fun back.
Glacier is cool. But Cosmic Orange is a legend. It’s going to be hard for Apple to come up with another color that has the same impact.

				
					

				
			Cosmic Orange clashes with Apple’s Crisp Blue iPhone 18 Pro Max Silicone Case with MagSafe, but maybe that’s how you roll.

title: This clever workaround lets iPhone 18 Pro Max skirt battery shipping max power limits
content:
The iPhone 18 Pro Max has a battery with more capacity than permitted to ship. To get around that, Apple is using a combination of hardware, software, and user authentication to slip under the regulatory wire.

iPhone 18 Pro Max
Customers began receiving devices on September 18. An Apple support document published the same day explains why the iPhone 18 Pro Max arrives with a battery capacity restriction in place.
At full capacity, the iPhone 18 Pro Max battery exceeds 20 watt-hours, putting it above a threshold that brings extra shipping requirements in most countries and regions. Apple uses firmware to keep the battery below 20 Wh while the phone moves through its factory and shipping network.
The restriction disappears automatically once the owner activates the iPhone, restoring access to the battery's full rated capacity, reports The Verge on Monday.

title: Best Mac 2026: Every Apple Mac and MacBook compared
content:

Which Mac is best for you? 
Whether you want everyday portability, professional creative power, desktop performance, or budget-friendly computing, Apple’s lineup has a Mac that fits. For $699 you can own a MacBook Neo, which is Apple’s most affordable laptop. Spend a little more and the MacBook Air excels at everyday work and battery life, while the MacBook Pro lineup delivers the extra power required by demanding professional workloads. If you prefer a desktop, the iMac is a great all-in-one option for the home, while Mac mini offers good value if you don’t need portability and already have a display and accessories. At the top end, the Mac Studio is built for intensive professional workloads, including demanding creative work and AI development.
Choosing the best Mac in 2026 isn’t simply about buying the newest model; it’s about finding the Mac that best matches what you need from a computer. Apple’s lineup ranges from ultraportable MacBooks to powerful desktop Macs, with options for students, everyday users, creatives and professionals.
In this Mac buying guide, we cover everything you need to know about the MacBook Neo, MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, Mac mini, iMac and Mac Studio, including the differences in size, specs, features and price. We’ll help you decide which Mac and configuration offers the right balance of value, performance and portability for you.
Best Mac 2026: Mac & MacBook Buyers Guide
Our top Mac for most people in 2026 is the MacBook Air. It offers an excellent combination of performance, portability and value in a compact package that will suit the typical Mac user.
If you need more power, we recommend the MacBook Pro, which delivers high-end performance in a portable form. At the other end of the price range, the new MacBook Neo starts at $699/£699 and is Apple’s most affordable Mac laptop.
If you don’t need a laptop, Apple also has some excellent desktop options. The Mac Studio offers exceptional performance for the money and can save thousands compared with a similarly specified Mac laptop, while the Mac mini is Apple’s cheapest desktop Mac, starting at $899/£899.
Below, we take you through every Mac currently available from Apple, explaining who each model is best suited to and what you should consider when choosing a configuration. Price increases June 2026
In June 2026, Apple increased prices significantly across several product lines including Macs, iPads, the Apple TV 4K, and HomePod models, citing an unprecedented rise in component costs. 
The company stated it had “never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly” and that it had shielded customers from these increases for as long as possible before finally raising prices.

Additional options: M5 Pro with 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU; 48GB or 64GB unified memory; up to 8TB SSD, and 10Gb Ethernet
The Mac mini does not include a display, keyboard, or mouse, so you’ll have to provide your own, or you can customize your order to include these devices as extra-cost options.
How do I connect stuff? The M5 Pro Mac mini has two USB-C/USB 3 ports and a headphone jack on the front. On the back are three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI and Ethernet. Thunderbolt 5 offers transfer speeds up to 120Gbps and can also be used for display, storage, docks and other high-performance peripherals. It can drive up to three 6K displays. Wireless connectivity is Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, while wired networking is now 2.5Gb Ethernet as standard, with 10Gb Ethernet available as an option. Apple has also introduced genlock over USB-C, which will be useful in professional video setups where cameras and displays need to be synchronized.
How fast is it?  The M5 Pro offers up to an 18-core CPU, 20-core GPU and 307GB/s memory bandwidth, versus the M6’s 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU and 170GB/s. That makes M5 Pro better suited to demanding video, 3D, development and local AI workloads. Apple claims the M5 Pro Mac mini offers up to 4x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio, 1.4x faster ray-traced rendering in Blender, and 1.5x faster image processing in Affinity compared to the M4 Pro Mac mini.
Any other considerations? Memory and storage can’t be upgraded later, so choose carefully; for demanding work, extra unified memory is worth prioritizing. You’ll also need your own display, keyboard and mouse. The M6 Mac mini is cheaper and powerful enough for most users, while those needing substantially more performance should consider the Mac Studio. Display, keyboard and mouse not included.
Why we recommend the Mac mini (M5 Pro): It’s not as affordable as it once was, but the M5 Pro Mac mini packs impressive professional-level performance into an exceptionally small desktop. Compared with the M6 model, it offers more CPU and GPU cores, almost twice the memory bandwidth, up to 64GB unified memory, Thunderbolt 5, and support for three 6K displays. For developers, video editors, 3D artists, and demanding AI workloads, it’s a good middle ground between the standard Mac mini and the more expensive Mac Studio.

What is it? The Mac Studio with M5 Max is Apple’s high-performance compact desktop for professional users. It between the Mac mini with M5 Pro and the more expensive M5 Ultra version of the Mac Studio. It doesn’t come with a display, keyboard or mouse, but its small desktop design packs in considerably more sustained performance and connectivity than Apple’s laptops. The M5 Max version supports up to 128GB of unified memory and five external displays.
What’s new? Apple updated the Mac Studio in August 2026, replacing the M4 Max chip in the model introduced in March 2025 with the M5 Max. The design hasn’t changed, but there are significant upgrades inside. The M5 Max has an 18-core CPU and up to 40-core GPU, with Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core for much faster AI processing. Memory bandwidth increases to as much as 614GB/s, storage is up to twice as fast, and the Mac Studio gains Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Apple has also added support for genlock over USB-C and Thunderbolt 5 clustering, which allows multiple Mac Studios to work together on distributed AI workloads.
Who’s it for? The Mac Studio with M5 Max is aimed at creative and technical professionals who need more performance than a Mac mini can provide, but don’t need the extreme power – or price – of the M5 Ultra. Apple specifically highlights musicians, photographers, software developers, engineers and designers working with 3D and motion graphics. It’s also a strong choice for video editing, software development, AI image and video generation, and running large language models locally. If your work involves exceptionally large AI models, complex VFX simulations or huge quantities of 8K video, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio may be more appropriate.
How much does the Mac Studio cost? The M5 Max Mac Studio starts at $2,499/£2,499. That gets you the M5 Max with an 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory and 512GB SSD. The starting price hasn’t changed from the price Apple introduced in June 2026, but it is substantially higher than the previous model’s original launch price: the M4 Max Mac Studio started at $1,999/£2,099 when it arrived in March 2025.
What are the specifications? The entry-level M5 Max Mac Studio offers:
Apple M5 Max, 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 512GB SSD, $2,499/£2,499.
Additional options: M5 Max SoC with a 18-core CPU, up to a 40-core GPU; up to 128GB unified memory; up to 8TB SSD storage.
The memory bandwidth of the M5 Max is 614GB compared to 546GB/s for the M4 Max model.
How do I connect stuff? The M5 Max Mac Studio has the following ports:
Four Thunderbolt 5 ports on the back supporting speeds of up to 120Gb/s.
Two USB-C ports on the front (these are Thunderbolt on the M5 Ultra model).
SDXC Card slot on the front.
Two USB-A ports.
10Gb ethernet.
HDMI.
3.5 mm headphone jack
Wi-Fi 7.
Bluetooth 6.
The M5 Max supports up to five external displays. The Mac Studio doesn’t include a display, keyboard or mouse, so you’ll need to provide your own or add Apple’s as extra-cost options.
How fast is it? The M5 Max Mac Studio is significantly faster than the previous M4 Max model, with some of the biggest improvements coming in AI workloads. Apple says LLM prompt processing in LM Studio can be up to 3.9x faster than M4 Max, while text-to-image generation can be up to 3.5x faster. Magic Mask processing in DaVinci Resolve Studio is up to 3x faster, while Redshift scene rendering is up to 1.4x faster. Apple also says the new GPU can be up to 50 percent faster than the previous generation for graphics-intensive work. The 18-core CPU is also faster than the M4 Max and memory bandwidth rises to 614GB/s. The M5 Max can simultaneously play as many as 19 streams of 8K ProRes 422 video at 30fps. The Mac Studio’s active cooling also means it is designed to maintain this level of performance during long, intensive workloads.
Any other considerations? The M5 Max is an extremely powerful chip – if you don’t regularly perform processor-, graphics- or AI-intensive work, a Mac mini will probably offer better value. The main disadvantage is that the Mac Studio is just the computer: you’ll need to provide a display, keyboard and mouse or trackpad, which can add considerably to the overall cost if you don’t already own them. You should also choose your memory and internal storage carefully when you order because neither can be upgraded later.
Why we recommend the Mac Studio (M5 Max): The Mac Studio with M5 Max strikes a strong balance between performance and price for professionals who rely on processor- and graphics-intensive apps. Its 18-core CPU, powerful GPU, up to 128GB of unified memory and high memory bandwidth make it well suited to video editing, 3D rendering, software development, music production and AI workloads, especially if you regularly spend time waiting for projects to render, compile or export.
At $2,499/£2,499 it isn’t cheap, and you’ll still need to provide a display and peripherals, but it offers substantially more performance than the Mac mini while costing far less than the $5,499/£5,499 M5 Ultra model. With the Mac Pro discontinued, the Mac Studio is now Apple’s highest-performance desktop and the best fit for many creative professionals, developers, engineers and other power users. What is it? The Mac Studio with M5 Ultra is Apple’s most powerful Mac and its highest-end desktop. The M5 Ultra chip combines two M5 Max dies using Apple’s UltraFusion architecture, giving it significantly more CPU and GPU cores, memory capacity and bandwidth than the M5 Max model. It is designed for workloads that would overwhelm most Macs, including complex 3D rendering, multiple streams of 8K video, scientific simulations and running very large AI models locally.
What’s new? Apple introduced the M5 Ultra Mac Studio on August 25, 2026, replacing the M3 Ultra model that arrived in March 2025. The headline change is the M5 Ultra chip, which offers up to a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU, with a Neural Accelerator in every GPU core. Memory bandwidth rises from 819GB/s on M3 Ultra to 1.2TB/s, while maximum unified memory remains 512GB. Apple has also introduced faster PCIe Gen 6-based SSD storage, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and genlock over USB-C. The external design is unchanged.
Who’s it for? The M5 Ultra Mac Studio is for people with exceptionally demanding professional workloads. That includes VFX artists rendering complex scenes, filmmakers working with multiple streams of high-resolution video, engineers running simulations, and AI researchers or data scientists working with very large models. Its ability to support as much as 512GB of unified memory is particularly significant for AI developers who want to run huge LLMs locally rather than rely on cloud services. Most users, including many creative professionals, will find the considerably cheaper M5 Max Mac Studio more than powerful enough.
How much does the Mac Studio cost? The Mac Studio with M5 Ultra starts at $5,499/£5,499, with a 30-core CPU, 64-core GPU, 96GB unified memory and 1TB SSD. That is $200/£200 more than the M3 Ultra model cost immediately before it was replaced, and $1,500 more than the $3,999 launch price of the previous-generation M3 Ultra Mac Studio when it was introduced in March 2025. There are a number of build-to-order options, including a 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU, and 16TB SSD. There was also a 512GB Unified Memory option, but memory shortages mean that won’t be available until October 2026. A Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, 16TB SSD and 256GB unified memory costs $18,299, the 512GB RAM option will cost even more when it is available.
What are the specifications? The Mac Studio with Mac Ultra processor offers these specs:
Apple M5 Ultra, 30-core CPU, 64-core GPU, 96GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, $5,499/£5,499
Additional options: M5 Ultra with 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU, up to 512GB unified memory (October onwards), and up to 16TB SSD.
The memory bandwidth of the M5 Ultra is 1.2TB/s compared to 819GB/s in the M3 Ultra model.
How do I connect stuff? The Mac Studio has the following ports:
Four Thunderbolt 5 ports on the back supporting speeds of up to 120Gb/s.
Two Thunderbolt 5 ports on the front.
SDXC Card slot on the front.
Two USB-A ports.
10Gb ethernet.
HDMI.
3.5 mm headphone jack
Wi-Fi 7.
Bluetooth 6.
The M5 Ultra Mac Studio supports up to eight external displays at 6K and 60Hz, or up to four displays at 5K and 120Hz. The Mac Studio does not include a display, keyboard, or mouse, so you’ll have to provide your own, or you can customize your order to include these devices as extra-cost options.
How fast is it? Apple says the M5 Ultra delivers up to 1.3x faster multithreaded CPU performance, 1.8x faster graphics and 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of the M3 Ultra. Compared with M1 Ultra, Apple claims up to 2.4x faster CPU performance, 4.7x faster GPU performance and 9.8x faster AI performance. In specific workloads, Apple claims up to 3.3x faster ML training in Foundry Nuke, 4x faster LLM processing in LM Studio, 4.3x faster text-to-image generation and 1.7x faster Redshift rendering. SSD performance can also be up to twice as fast as the previous generation.
Any other considerations? The biggest consideration is whether you actually need this much performance. At $5,499/£5,499 before any upgrades, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio costs $3,000/£3,000 more than the entry-level M5 Max Mac Studio. The M5 Max model is already an extremely powerful workstation and will be sufficient for many video editors, developers, photographers and other creative professionals. If you do need large amounts of unified memory, remember that memory and internal storage cannot be upgraded after purchase, so choose your configuration carefully. Display, keyboard and mouse not included.
Why we recommend the Mac Studio M5 Ultra: The M5 Ultra Mac Studio is excessive for most people, but that is the point. It offers the highest CPU core count in any Mac, Apple’s most powerful GPU, up to 512GB of unified memory and an extraordinary 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth in a compact desktop. The jump in AI performance makes it particularly compelling for developers and researchers who need to run extremely large models locally, while its 80-core GPU, powerful media engines and extensive Thunderbolt 5 connectivity make it equally well suited to demanding video, VFX and 3D workflows. If your work can actually take advantage of that hardware, this is the most powerful Mac you can buy.

What is it? The iMac is what Apple is famous for, although the current design is as far removed from the original as you can get. It’s the Mac to have in a living room or an office reception – somewhere you can show it off.
What’s new? In October 2024 Apple introduced the M4 version of the 24-inch iMac. Little has changed since the redesign of 2021, which represented the first major update in more than a decade, with a cleaner design and a choice of seven bright colors (slightly lighter shades for 2024).
Who’s it for? The iMac is great for both novices and demanding users. It can handle general-purpose and heavy-duty tasks equally well, although those after a replacement for a 27-inch IMac or iMac Pro might want to wait to see if the rumored iMac Pro ever materializes, or settle for a Mac mini Pro or Mac Studio. It’s ideal for someone who needs to buy a complete computer setup (keyboard, mouse or trackpad, and display) and wants to maximize workspace efficiency. The 24-inch iMac is a design icon that will look great in any office.
How much does the iMac cost? Following the June price hikes, the three standard configurations start at $1,499/£1,499 (up from $1,299/£1,299) for the entry-level model, and $1,699/£1,699 (up from $1,499/£1,499) for the mid-range.
What are the specifications? The 24-inch iMac still uses Apple’s M4 chip. Compared to other Macs, there is half the storage as standard, at 256GB. There are several configurations available as well as build-to-order options:
Apple M4, 8-core CPU, 8-core GPU, 16GB memory, 256GB SSD, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, $1,499/£1,499.
Apple M4, 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, 16GB memory, 256GB SSD, four Thunderbolt 4 ports, $1,699/£1,699.
Apple M4, 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, 16GB memory, 512GB SSD, four Thunderbolt 4 ports, $1,899/£1,899.
Apple M4, 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, 24GB memory, 512GB SSD, four Thunderbolt 4 ports, $2,099/£2,099.
Additional options: 32GB memory; up to 2TB storage
What are the display specifications? The 24-inch 4.5K Retina display has 11.3 million pixels and supports the P3 wide color gamut, over a billion colors, 500 nits of brightness, and True Tone. Apple treats the display with an anti-reflective coating to help with readability. The display hasn’t changed since the M1 model launched.
How do I connect stuff? The $1,499 24-inch iMac has two Thunderbolt 4 ports that also work with USB-C devices. The $1,699 and $1,899 iMacs have four Thunderbolt 4 ports (the previous generation had two Thunderbolt/USB 4 and two USB 3 ports). If you have a USB-A device, you need to buy an adapter, such as Apple’s ($19 / £19). If you have multiple USB-A devices and other items, consider a Thunderbolt hub. The 24-inch iMac also has a headphone jack on the side.
Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3 are built-in. Apple doesn’t put a gigabit ethernet port on the 24-inch iMac—instead, it’s on the power adapter. But that ethernet-equipped power adapter comes standard with the $1,699 and $1,899 models. It’s not included with the $1,499 model, but you can select it as an option at the point of purchase—and yes, that means you’ll have to pay extra for it.
How fast is it?: The 24-inch iMac is the only Mac still using the M4 chip, so it’s not as fast as the other Macs, but it’s still got all the speed general consumers need, and it can even handle pro applications with no problem. However, the $1,499 model has only one fan inside its body, while the $1,699 and $1,899 models have two fans. That means the high-priced models do a better job of keeping the internals cool. The $1,499 model may need to slow down its performance on heavy-duty tasks in order to maintain a proper temperature.
Any other considerations? The iMac doesn’t represent particularly good value at its current price. A better buy is the MacBook Air, which offers a faster M5 chip with a 10-core CPU, 8-core GPU, 16GB of memory, and a 512GB SSD for $1,299/£1,299. By comparison, the iMac costs $1,499/£1,499 yet includes an older M4 chip with an 8-core CPU, 8-core GPU, the same 16GB of memory, and only a 256GB SSD. We feel that the iMac price is high compared to the specs on offer, but we do admire the design. We are holding out for a bigger screen. Apple is rumored to launch an M6 iMac in 2027.
Why we recommend the iMac (M4): The iMac was transformed when Apple introduced the redesigned 24-inch model in 2021, with major improvements to its design, display, and performance. If you’re buying one today, the $1,699/£1,699 model is the sweet spot, adding more ports, Touch ID, and Ethernet. We’d still love to see Apple revive the iMac Pro with a larger display, and sincerely hope one is in the pipeline.

 FAQ 


1.
What’s best, MacBook Air or MacBook Pro?
We address this question in detail in our comparison of the MacBook Air vs Pro. It’s really a question of price versus power. The Air is sufficient for most people’s needs, the Pro will give you that extra boost in terms of what the Mac is capable of.
Buying an entry-level MacBook Air for $1,299/£1,299 will get you an excellent Mac laptop. If you want to spend less than that you may be able to find a discounted MacBook Air – we round up the best MacBook Air deals regularly.
If you want a larger screen, the 15-inch MacBook Air is a great option that is a lot cheaper than the smaller 14-inch MacBook Pro. 
The price of the Pro and Max MacBook Pro models is high, but these models offer the kind of specs professional users, especially creatives, need, including support for more RAM, and more CPU and GPU cores. If you can afford to stretch to the Max you will get the ultimate Mac without a doubt, but you need to be willing to make a significant investment.
The choice between the 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro is all down to the screen size. The 16-inch models are more expensive, but once you spec them out in such a way to be comparable the price difference is minor. The bigger difference is between the Pro and Max processors. Other than speed, MacBooks with Max processors can connect up to four external displays (three over Thunderbolt and one over HDMI), while since the M4 all models allow two external displays in addition to the laptop screen. (There are workarounds if you need to connect more screens).
There is now another Mac laptop to consider, the MacBook Neo lowers the price of ownership of a Mac laptop to $699/£699. If budget really is tight though, you might want to consider a discounted previous generation MacBook Air instead.





2.
Should I upgrade from my Intel Mac?
Yes. It’s time! We are now more than six years into Apple’s transition from Intel processors to its own silicon that includes CPU, GPU, and unified memory. The transition began with the introduction of the M1 in November 2020. Since June 2023 every Mac Apple sells uses Apple’s own chips rather than Intel processors.
If you’ve yet to upgrade your Intel Mac to one powered by Apple’s silicon what are you waiting for? If you are concerned that a must-have app doesn’t run on an M-series Mac, consider finding a new app because the performance gains are tremendous.
Another good reason to replace an Intel Mac is that Apple’s support for these models is winding down. macOS Golden Gate, released in September 2026, is the first major version of macOS to support no Intel Macs. Intel Macs compatible with older versions of macOS may continue receiving security updates for a limited period, but they are now outside Apple’s current feature-release cycle. Apple does not guarantee how long those updates will continue, and machines limited to macOS Sequoia are likely to lose support sooner than those capable of running macOS Tahoe. Read: How long does Apple support Macs.





3.
Where can I get the best price for a new Mac?
Apple rarely offers direct price cuts on new hardware, but resellers frequently do. Getting the best price on a new Mac requires knowing where to look and when to buy: 
Top U.S. Retailers:
Amazon: Often has the lowest prices, especially during events like Prime Day. For example, during the July 2026 Prime Day event, a 14-inch M5 MacBook Pro was available for $1,749, a $450 discount. Even outside of events, Amazon frequently undercuts Apple’s MSRP.
Best Buy: A reliable source for discounts and trade-in offers. In late 2025, Best Buy offered a massive $1,150 off an M2 Ultra Mac Studio.
B&H Photo: A well-regarded authorized reseller that often has competitive pricing on Macs.
Walmart: Known for exclusive deals on older models, like the M1 MacBook Air, which has been sold brand-new for just $599.
Top U.K. Retailers:
Amazon UK: Similar to the U.S., Amazon UK is a primary source for discounts.
KRCS: An Apple Premium Reseller that frequently offers good deals.
John Lewis & Currys: Reliable high-street retailers that often have competitive prices and good customer service.
If you’re looking for a great offer, visit our MacBook Pro deals, MacBook Air deals, iMac deals, Mac Studio deals, and Mac mini deals pages which are regularly updated.





4.
What specs do I really need for my Mac?
Chip: The specs you need depend on what you plan to do with your Mac. For everyday tasks such as web browsing, email, office apps and light photo editing, a standard M-series chip is more than sufficient. Apple’s latest entry-level desktop chip is the M6, available in the Mac mini, while other Macs still use M4 or M5-generation chips. 
If you regularly work with complex spreadsheets, large Photoshop files, audio projects, video editing or more demanding games, look at a Pro chip. The M5 Pro Mac mini, for example, offers up to an 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU and up to 64GB unified memory.
For professional video production, 3D work, software development and other intensive workloads, a Max chip is more appropriate. The Mac Studio with M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU, up to a 40-core GPU and as much as 128GB unified memory. 
The M5 Ultra, with up to a 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU and 512GB unified memory, is aimed at the most extreme workloads, including VFX, scientific computing and running very large AI models locally.
GPU: One of the biggest differences between Apple’s chips is GPU performance. Standard M-series chips are easily sufficient for everyday graphics, casual gaming and light creative work. Pro chips add considerably more GPU power for video editing, graphics work, 3D applications and gaming. Max chips are designed for professional graphics, high-resolution video and demanding 3D workflows, while Ultra provides Apple’s highest GPU performance. The M5 Max offers up to 40 GPU cores, while the M5 Ultra doubles that to 80 GPU cores. Both also have Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core to speed up AI workloads.
RAM: Apple calls RAM Unified Memory. The MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB, which is probably the biggest drawback of that machine. Most Macs start with at least 16GB, which is plenty for everyday use, although we recommend choosing more if your budget allows because the memory cannot be upgraded later. 24GB or 32GB is a good choice for heavier multitasking, photo editing, podcasting, moderate video production and gaming. Developers and professional creative users may benefit from 48GB, 64GB or more. The new M5 Pro Mac mini can be configured with up to 64GB, M5 Max Mac Studio with up to 128GB, and M5 Ultra Mac Studio with an enormous 512GB.
Storage: Even with iCloud and external drives available, it can seem like you can never have enough storage inside your Mac. 256GB may be sufficient for basic web and office use, but it can fill up quickly. We recommend 512GB for most people who want to keep a Mac for several years, particularly if you store photos, games or media locally. For regular video or audio production, 1TB or more is preferable. Professional users may need several terabytes: the M5 Pro Mac mini can be configured with up to 8TB, while Mac Studio configurations go even higher. As with unified memory, internal Mac storage cannot be upgraded after purchase, so it is worth thinking about future requirements when ordering.
For more information to help you decide which Mac to buy see our Mac processor comparison where we compare Apple silicon and Intel. We also offer advice about how much storage, RAM, and cores in How much MacBook RAM, SSD, GPU, and CPU do you really need.





5.
When were the Macs last updated?
In August 2026 the Mac mini and Mac Studio were updated. 
In March 2026 the MacBook Pro and MacBook Air were updated, and the MacBook Neo was introduced.
The most recent iMac update was in October 2024.
The Mac Pro has been discontinued. 





Why you can trust Macworld’s advice
Macworld has been covering everything Apple related since our first issue which arrived alongside the original Mac in 1984. Nobody knows Apple better, except probably Apple, but the difference is that we are completely impartial. We are made up of a team of experts with decades of experiences with Macs and other Apple products, and between us we have reviewed every Apple product meaning we are uniquely positioned to provide buying advice.

title: Should you buy a Mac Studio now? M5 Max vs M5 Ultra buying advice
content:
Macworld





Apple announced the new M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studio on August 25, with shipping from September 22. As the Mac Studio has just received a major update, this is generally a good time to buy if you need a powerful professional desktop.
For most buyers, we recommend the M5 Max Mac Studio (reviewed here). Starting at $2,499/£2,499, it provides more than enough performance for professional video editing, software development, music production, photography and 3D work, with up to 128GB of unified memory.
The M5 Ultra Mac Studio starts at $5,499/£5,499 and is intended for exceptionally demanding workloads, including very large local AI models, complex scientific computing, high-end VFX and large-scale 3D rendering. Most professionals will not need to spend this much.
The new models ship from September 22, although the M5 Ultra configuration with 512GB of unified memory will not be available until late October.


Should you buy a Mac Studio now or wait?
There are reasons to wait before buying the Mac Studio. Discounts may improve in the months after launch, particularly around Black Friday at the end of November, while reduced or refurbished M4 Max and M3 Ultra models may become available as buyers upgrade. If your current Mac still meets your needs, you want to see independent benchmarks or you’re looking for the lowest possible price, there is no need to rush.
However, waiting carries some risk. Memory shortages caused long delivery times and limited availability for the previous generation, and similar constraints could affect popular M5 Max and M5 Ultra configurations. The new Mac Studio with 512GB of unified memory is already delayed until late October, while other build-to-order configurations may also take longer to arrive.
Buy now if…
You need workstation-class Mac performance.
You are replacing an Intel Mac or an older Mac Studio.
Your work benefits from sustained CPU, GPU or Media Engine performance.
You need Thunderbolt 5, 10Gb Ethernet or extensive display support.
The M5 Max supplies all the performance and memory you need.
Consider M5 Ultra if…
You need more than 128GB of unified memory.
You work with enormous local AI models or datasets.
You need the highest possible GPU or multithreaded CPU performance.
You require up to eight external displays.
Your work can make use of its additional media engines and 1.2TB/s memory bandwidth.
Wait if…
Your current Mac Studio still handles your workload comfortably.
You want independent benchmarks before spending $2,499 or more.
You need the 512GB M5 Ultra configuration, which arrives in late October.
You are hoping for M4 Max or M3 Ultra clearance/refurbished prices.
You don’t need a new workstation urgently.


						

							




		
Apple Mac Studio (M5 Max, 2026)

Apple Mac Studio (M5 Ultra, 2026)

Which Mac Studio to buy: Max vs Ultra?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The primary difference between the Mac Studio Ultra and Max models lies in the processing architecture, where the Ultra chip essentially combines two Max chips into a single die to provide roughly double the performance cores and graphical power. The choice between the two comes down to the intensity of your workflow. 
Mac Studio (M5 Max): Best for most professionals
The M5 Max Mac Studio offers a lower entry price and is the model most buyers should choose.
It’s ideal for:
Video editing
Software development
Music production
Photography and design work
General professional workloads
Starting at $2,499, it delivers workstation-class performance without the significant premium commanded by Ultra models.
Mac Studio (M5 Ultra): Best for extreme workloads
The M5 Ultra, starting at $5,499, is designed for users who regularly push hardware to its limits.
It’s best suited to:
Large AI models
Professional 3D rendering
Scientific computing
Massive video-production projects
Heavily multi-threaded workloads
The M5 Ultra architecture provides substantially more CPU and GPU resources, higher memory ceilings, and greater expansion potential than the M5 Max.
However, most professionals will not fully utilise its additional performance.


						

							


Mac Studio vs Mac mini: Which is best?
Many buyers should also consider the considerably less expensive Mac mini M5 Pro.
Mac mini M5 Pro starts at $1,699/£1,699.
Mac Studio M5 Max starts at $2,499/£2,499.
Will the M5 Pro Mac mini meet your workload, or will the Mac Studio’s additional GPU performance, memory and connectivity save enough working time to justify the extra $800/£800?
The Mac mini offers better value if its GPU performance and maximum 64GB of unified memory are sufficient for your needs. The Mac Studio provides a substantially more powerful GPU, up to 128GB of unified memory with M5 Max, four rear Thunderbolt 5 ports, 10Gb Ethernet as standard and support for up to five displays. The M5 Pro Mac mini has three Thunderbolt 5 ports, optional 10Gb Ethernet and supports up to three displays.
The Mac Studio is worth the extra cost if you need:
Greater GPU performance
More than 64GB of unified memory
More Thunderbolt connectivity
Support for more than three displays
Faster performance in demanding video, 3D or AI workloads
10Gb Ethernet without paying for an upgrade
Both Macs support Thunderbolt 5, which offers substantially more bandwidth than Thunderbolt 4. It is particularly useful for:
High-speed external SSDs and storage arrays
Professional video editing and post-production
Multiple high-resolution displays
High-bandwidth docks and expansion systems
Moving very large media, development or AI datasets
For coding, general productivity and moderately demanding creative work, the M5 Pro Mac mini is likely to offer better value. The Mac Studio makes more sense for sustained professional workloads that can take advantage of its additional GPU cores, media engines, memory and connectivity.

What specifications should you choose?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Here is some guidance on which specifications to select.
RAM
Memory is more important than processor upgrades for many buyers.
36GB: Suitable for many professional photography, music, development and mainstream video workflows.
48GB or 64GB: A sensible choice for heavier multitasking, larger development projects, 4K/8K video and more complex creative work.
128GB: For demanding M5 Max workflows, larger local AI models and projects that regularly create significant memory pressure.
96GB M5 Ultra: The entry point for buyers whose workload genuinely benefits from Ultra.
256GB or 512GB: Specialist options for enormous AI models, datasets, simulations and high-end VFX—not conventional future-proofing.
Storage
Internal storage can be supplemented with external Thunderbolt drives, making it easier to expand later.
For most professional users:
512GB is usable but restrictive for a $2,499 workstation.
1TB is a more practical starting point for most professionals.
External Thunderbolt 5 storage can provide cheaper project and archive capacity.
Internal storage is preferable for applications, caches, active datasets and workflows that depend on maximum SSD performance. M5 Max supports up to 8TB; M5 Ultra supports up to 16TB.



							


Other things to consider when buying a Mac Studio
Neither the Mac mini nor the Mac Studio includes a display, keyboard or mouse. A professional monitor and other peripherals can add significantly to the total cost, so factor these into your budget.
If you’re buying for the long term:
Prioritize unified memory, because it cannot be upgraded later.
Choose enough internal storage for your essential apps and active projects, while remembering that external storage can be added later.
Buy the configuration that meets your likely needs without paying for performance you will rarely use.
If a replacement is expected soon, consider whether waiting makes sense – particularly if you plan to keep the Mac for five years or more.

title: New Mac Studio's Biggest Upgrade Isn't the M5 Ultra Chip, Review Says
content:
Ahead of the new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips launching this Tuesday, the first reviews of the computer have been shared by selected tech websites and YouTube channels. According to one review published by Macworld's Roman Loyola, the biggest upgrade isn't even the M5 Ultra, but rather significantly faster storage speeds.


"Typically, we start our reviews by looking at overall performance with Geekbench, and then we work our way through more specific aspects," he said. "But the SSD performance is so overwhelmingly good, it's the story here."

Loyola ran Blackmagic's Disk Speed Test benchmark tool on the new Mac Studio with an 18-core M5 Max chip, 128GB of RAM, and a 4TB SSD, and the computer achieved around 2.6× faster SSD read speeds and around 2.1× faster SSD write speeds compared to a previous-generation Mac Studio with the M4 Max chip. The results are shown in the image below.


Indeed, Apple advertised up to 2× faster storage speeds for the new Mac Studio, and these benchmark results show an even bigger boost. As always, real-world performance may vary, but expect significantly faster SSD speeds overall.

already surfaced last week if you are interested in that.

Unsurprisingly, the M5 Ultra is Apple's fastest chip ever. Based on Geekbench 7 results so far, it has up to around 30% faster single-core CPU performance and up to around 35% faster multi-core performance compared to the M3 Ultra.

Apple said the M5 Ultra has up to 1.25× faster single-threaded CPU performance and up to 1.3× faster multi-threaded CPU performance compared to the M3 Ultra, so the benchmark results roughly align with or even beat those advertised claims.

The Verge's Antonio G. Di Benedetto describing the M5 Ultra model's performance as "outrageous" and PCMag's Brian Westover calling the computer "a serious powerhouse for top-tier local AI inference."
